title: edh-tool
kind: Full-stack web app · AI data pipeline
hook: Popularity-ranked deck tools steer every Commander player toward the same cards. edh-tool uses AI-tagged card data to find the strong ones nobody is playing.

facts.problem: Sites like EDHREC rank cards by how often they're already played, so a strong card nobody has heard of looks exactly like a weak one. Players end up building the same decks.
facts.built: An offline Python pipeline that has Claude tag each card against an 80-tag vocabulary and write themes for each commander, a dependency-free JavaScript scoring engine, and a Next.js site with theme recommendations, a browser-based deck builder, and Moxfield/Archidekt export.
facts.role: Solo developer, with Claude Code as a pair-programmer: product design, the AI pipeline, the scoring model, and the full-stack site, from Postgres schema to UI. I compared models against a hand-tagged set before committing to the full run.
facts.outcome: 12,580 cards tagged and 4,463 themes generated across 792 commanders, live at edh-tool.com. Trimming the model's output format cut output tokens by 68% while still matching hand tags just as closely, bringing the full tagging run to $12.41.

details.heading: One scoring engine everywhere
details.body: Each card's score is fit × commander synergy × quality × popularity × art match, computed by a single pure-JS module that runs in the API routes, the CLI, the tuning bench, and the tests, so a score on the site is the same score everywhere. Five picks per theme are drawn by seeded weighted sampling, so a player's list stays stable while they build, and two players with the same commander still see different cards.

details.heading: Separating unknown from bad
details.body: The obscurity bonus uses log rank, because popularity follows a power law, and it's gated by the model's quality estimate so obscure junk never gets lifted. Across 200 simulated players, each theme surfaces 21–40 distinct cards.

details.heading: Choosing the model with data
details.body: Sonnet and Haiku tagged the same 221 cards and were scored against hand tags. Haiku found tags about as often but rated weak cards 0.59 versus Sonnet's 0.34, which would have broken the gem filter. I picked Sonnet and cut cost with the Batch API and a slimmer output format instead of a smaller model.

title: Live Trading Screen
hook: Market data arrives far faster than a screen can draw it. This real-time trading screen stays responsive at up to 17,000 order-book updates per second.

facts.problem: A trading UI that redraws on every market message either crashes from cross-thread access or freezes under thousands of queued UI calls per second.
facts.built: A read-only Windows trading screen with a hand-drawn price chart, an order-book ladder, and a watchlist, fed by Kraken's live WebSocket order books or an offline simulator. Plain-English labels throughout make it readable for someone who has never traded.
facts.role: Solo developer, with Claude Code as a pair-programmer. I set the product direction and the core architecture, made unit tests a requirement, and reviewed, ran, and QA'd the code against live data. It was my first WPF app and my first C# in over five years.
facts.outcome: The UI does the same work whether 60 or 17,000 updates arrive per second, and the chart draws in under 1 ms per frame. The 82 unit tests caught a real price-rounding bug on DOGE/USD during development.

details.heading: The UI pulls, the feed never pushes
details.body: A background thread keeps a private order book per market and, after every change, publishes an immutable snapshot by atomically replacing a dictionary entry. A 60 Hz timer on the UI thread is the only path to the screen, so there are no locks, no per-update dispatcher calls, and the UI can never see a half-updated book.

details.heading: Bounded by design
details.body: Price history is sampled at 10 Hz (about 3,000 points per market over 5 minutes), so memory and drawing cost don't grow with feed speed. Prices are stored as integer ticks so floating-point dust can't create duplicate levels.

details.heading: Hand-drawn controls
details.body: The chart (line and candlestick, crosshair, live time axis) and the ladder render directly in OnRender instead of thousands of per-cell elements, costing 0.5–0.8 ms of UI-thread time per frame. Live and simulated feeds sit behind one interface and are fully interchangeable.

title: Salmonid Data Sim & Visualizer
hook: Fish-passage counts are numbers in a spreadsheet. This turns ten seasons of real Snake River salmon data into a living underwater scene you can scrub through.

facts.problem: Columbia Basin Research's daily fish counts are public but dense, and hard to feel as anything more than a table.
facts.built: A Three.js flocking simulation of the salmon run passing Lower Granite Dam's underwater camera, with GPU caustics and light shafts, plus a HUD, season drawer, and labeled fish viewer driven by real daily counts.
facts.role: Solo developer, with Claude Code as a pair-programmer: concept, simulation, shaders, data wrangling, and UI.
facts.outcome: Ten counting seasons (2006–2015) swap in place from a season selector, with five tracked species driving the flock and each species drawn as a single instanced mesh.

details.heading: One sun, one light
details.body: The water's fresnel shading, the riverbed, the light shafts, the drifting silt, and the fish themselves all sample the same real-time caustics texture, so moving the sun slides one light net across the whole scene instead of several effects drifting out of sync.

details.heading: Cheap, believable motion
details.body: Flocking runs as 2D boids over a spatial grid, mapped to world X/Z only at render time. Each fish is a skinned mesh baked to a Vertex Animation Texture, with tailbeat rate derived from real per-fish swim speed.

details.heading: One timeline
details.body: The HUD chart, data drawer, and fish-viewer sparkline share one date-to-x mapping, so the scrubber never reads differently against two curves.
